Photograph: Altaf Hussain/Reuters View image in fullscreen Narendra Modi has never been challenged so publicly and so widely. Photograph: Altaf Hussain/Reuters First Edition newsletter India Monday briefing: ​How the Cockroach ​protests ​have expose​d the ​cracks in ​India’s government In today’s newsletter: Across ​the country, a ​younger generation is turning private disillusionment into public defiance​ against a government that once felt untouchable Hettie O'Brien Mon 27 Jul 2026 01.47 EDT Last modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 01.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. As flames engulfed parts of France and Spain this weekend, in India, the prime minister, Narendra Modi, was trying to put out a very different kind of fire. Thousands of people arrived in Delhi on Saturday to demand the resignation of his education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. When he stepped down in the early afternoon, the protests turned into a triumphant block party. But the Cockroach protests that have swept through India this summer are about much more than a single minister. They have humiliated Modi and undermined the indomitable power of his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) that has ruled India for the past 12 years. They’re also a lesson in using humour to political advantage. Modi likes to present himself as an infallible messiah , but young people have mocked the prime minister online and in the streets, calling him a “56-inch monkey” (a reference to Modi boasting about his ample 56-inch chest), and parodied his social media addresses. “Hating Modi is cool on the internet now, after years of criminalising dissent,” one told a reporter. Now the protesters have secured a victory, will their calls for revolution continue? For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to our south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen , who has been reporting on the “Cockroaches” in Delhi , about what their anger stems from and what it means for the BJP. That’s after a roundup of the biggest stories of the weekend. Weekend roundup Wild fires | Authorities in France battled to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux in the south-west as Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, warned Spain and the Iberian peninsula were suffering the effects of the climate emergency. Germany | A man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by police , German officials have said. Iran | The US has paused strikes on Iran for a second night as top military officials advised Donald Trump to halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war. UK politics | Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is to indicate he will put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations by taking up the country’s seat on the board at the World Bank. UK news | Five Palestine Action activists face being sentenced as terrorists for breaking windows and throwing red paint at a branch of Barclays Bank in Lancashire. In depth: ‘What if all cockroaches come together?’ View image in fullscreen The Cockroach Janta party has tasted victory and might widen the scope of the changes they seek. Photograph: Indranil Aditya/Reuters It started as a sardonic joke . On 16 May, Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student at Boston University, posted on X: “What if all cockroaches come together?” It was a tongue-in-cheek response to India’s chief justice, who had called unemployed young Indians “cockroaches”. Online, thousands of people responded to Dipke’s message. Realising he had tapped into something big, Dipke flew to Delhi on 6 June and went to Jantar Mantar, its famous protest ground. The protests drew young people from across the country, and the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) – a play on the BJP’s name – created a website listing their demands, including reform of India’s education system. India has a young population who are better educated than ever before, but it has proven a weak point for the BJP, with the country’s universities crumbling and its economy failing to provide jobs for many graduates. Millions of young people spend years prepping for gruelling public exams in the hope of securing a decent job, and their parents go into debt or sell their land to fund these studies. To make matters worse, these exam papers are routinely leaked and sold to the highest bidder. “Anyone rich enough can buy the answers,” Hannah tells me. This is devastating for millions of young people, forcing them to retake tests for which they’ve already studied. After a medical entrance exam was leaked in May, at least 12 students took their own lives; some left notes behind saying they could not bear the thought of resitting the test. The leaks are a potent symbol of institutional corruption, inflaming the anger that young people feel towards a political system that is failing them. Thief, thief Sonam Wangchuk, an engineer and education reformer from Ladakh, joined the protest on 28 June and declared he would go on indefinite hunger strike until the education minister resigned. “The idea of a hunger strike has a particularly powerful resonance in India,” says Hannah. “Gandhi put his life on the line several times with his hunger strikes for independence.” Delhi police forcibly removed Wangchuk from Jantar Mantar on 18 July and took him to hospital, supposedly for the sake of his health. Footage of his hospital stay went viral, and the Cockroach party called for a march on parliament. On Monday, tens of thousands of people started to fill Delhi’s streets. “In my whole time covering India, I’ve never seen so many people turning out,” Hannah says. The mood was jubilant, but by the afternoon, things had turned violent as the police began firing teargas and using batons on the protesters. Despite that, many of the protesters stayed put, and Hannah went back to Jantar Mantar in the following days. “It was the place to be in India,” she says. “There were people camping out, delivery guys bringing pizza and biryani, people cooking food. It had become about more than just the education minister resigning. More, even than education.” The protesters’ very public displays of contempt – graffiti of Modi’s name under the image of a urinating dog; people stamping on a poster of his face and chanting “thief, thief” – would have seemed unimaginable just two weeks ago. “People were just revelling in the opportunity to speak their mind,” Rahul Bhatia, a writer and author of The New India, who attended the protests on Saturday, tells me. “It was delightful. It made people think: things are possible.” Modi lost control of the narrative Pradhan’s resignation is a major victory for the Cockroach protesters. He is a Modi loyalist and former organiser for the RSS, the Hindu supremacist group closely affiliated with the BJP (for more on its sinister ideology, it’s worth reading this fascinating 2020 piece by Samanth Subramanian). “It creates a crack in the BJP’s armour,” Hannah says. Modi has projected an image of total authority, but this is one of the first instances where he has bent to popular will. He demands unflinching loyalty from his ministers. They may now be questioning whether their positions are quite as secure as they thought. India has taken a sharp turn towards autocracy under the BJP. Its main media channels are controlled by (or intensely favourable to) the government, and most of them gave minimal coverage to the protests, so young people resorted to sharing information and anti-government memes on social media. The party is no stranger to social media (its “troll army” is adept at smearing digital opponents, and the government tried to shut down the Cockroach party’s X account in early July), but it has lost control of the narrative. Modi’s last-ditch attempt to engage protesters with two reels he posted to his then 101 million Instagram followers on Thursday night (after which he gained over 1 million more, an impressive number, though still fewer than Beyoncé’s 299 million) seemed contrived and stilted. “He has been crucified online for those videos,” Hannah says. Is this the start of something bigger? It’s tempting to compare the Cockroach protests to other youth uprisings that have led to regime change in south Asia. But “a quick look at the outcome of people’s movements in India is not encouraging,” the novelist Arundhati Roy wrote in a recent piece for Equator magazine. “Revenge is surely being planned and will be visited on those [the government] sees as the main instigators.” After people took to the streets in 2019 to protest against the BJP’s controversial new citizenship act, the government swiftly outlawed gatherings in several places and detained protesters. The real test of the BJP’s power will come at election time. It is one of the world’s richest and most formidable parties, and has attempted to capture India’s electoral machinery, pushing for reforms to its voting map that would tilt power further in Modi’s favour. In West Bengal, a state the BJP had never won before, it “revised” the electoral roll and excluded more than 9.1 million voters from the register, securing a decisive victory earlier this year. “It seems like the BJP has much less support than people actually think,” Bhatia says. But after these protests, Modi will be doing all that he can to maintain his party’s grip on power. The week to come Monday | Andrew and Tristan Tate are due back in the Florida court where they’re fighting their extradition to the UK, to face rape and sex-trafficking charges. Tuesday | Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy are expected to be among those attending the Washington DC memorial service for the late South Carolina senator and Trump ally Lindsey Graham. Thursday | People will go to the polls to elect the next mayor of Greater Manchester, who will replace Andy Burnham. What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen Illustration: Guardian Design To enshittification, we can now add the idea of decadence without pleasure : “For anyone with an Internet connection and a little discretionary income, the contemporary moment offers a superabundance of seductive distractions. Why then the pervasive mood of emptiness ?” Truly, what a time to be alive. Toby Moses, head of newsletters The world is approaching “plutocratic collapse”. That’s the view of the French economist Gabriel Zucman , and I’m inclined to agree. I enjoyed Will Dunn’s recent profile of him in the New Statesman (£). Hettie Add shingles to the long list of things millennial women need to worry about – Emily Retter has looked at why the excruciating disease is on the rise. Photograph: Teresa Suárez/EPA Tour de France | Tadej Pogacar took a record-equalling fifth win in the Tour de France on Sunday, joining the all-time greats, as Mathieu van der Poel won a frantic final stage in Paris. Commonwealth Games | Adam Ramsay-Peaty is ready to bounce back after his 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games. He said: “The last 24 hours have been a bit of a whirlwind, but I’m really happy with that.” Formula One | Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix with an assured drive for McLaren at the Hungaroring, his and the team’s first victory of the year. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “Miliband vows to give UK ‘global leadership’ role on climate crisis”, is the Guardian ’s front page today. The Times says “Teen anxiety pays more than job”, and the Telegraph also has “PM to crack down on youth benefits”. Still on politics, The Mail goes with “Streeting: I will quit if defence plan falls short”, the i Paper says “Council tax and stamp duty to be scrapped under Burnham plans”, and the Express splashes “Police ‘waste’ millions on diversity schemes”. The FT splashes “Biggest defence companies home in on start-ups for nimbler military tech”, and the Mirror leads with its water safety campaign, saying “No child should die for a day at the seaside”. Lastly, Metro splashes “Fly and dry” on Gatwick’s water outage. Today in Focus View image in fullscreen The tech company’s relationship with the UK’s public health service is under the spotlight. Photograph: Arnd Wiegmann/Reuters How Palantir got into the NHS Investigative journalist, Lucas Amin, reports on how the tech company Palantir won a £330m contract with the NHS … and what happened once its software was introduced. Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld View image in fullscreen Illustration: Tom Gauld/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen The small clinical trial run by academics at Rutgers University in New Jersey found ‘additional benefits’ beyond weight loss to restricted eating. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian Restricting eating to a nine‑hour window and avoiding food for four hours before sleep may improve cognitive health in older adults . In a six‑month trial of 47 women who were considered overweight or obese, both groups lost similar weight, but those following time‑restricted eating performed better on spatial planning and problem‑solving tests, with hints of improved memory. Researchers suggest circadian rhythms, metabolism and inflammation may play a role. Experts stress the findings are preliminary and require larger, peer‑reviewed studies. Prof Wendy Hall, the head of nutritional sciences at King’s College London, said: “Time-restricted eating is a plausible approach to supporting cognitive health in midlife”. Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/AP View image in fullscreen Nirmal Purja pictured in 2021 after his return from leading the first team to summit K2 in winter. Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Mountaineering Top mountaineer Nirmal Purja confirmed dead after 11 hit by avalanche in Pakistan Other members of expedition led by world-renowned climber on Broad Peak have also died, climbing company says Geneva Abdul Sat 1 Aug 2026 09.41 EDT First published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 09.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A world-renowned Nepali mountaineer and former UK Special Forces member has died after being among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak. Nirmal Purja was killed leading an expedition of 10 other people on the world’s 12th-highest mountain when an avalanche struck at around noon on Thursday. Elite Exped, the company Purja co-founded, said in a statement: “Today it is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak.” “We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive,” it said, without further detail. Purja made history in 2019 after climbing all 14 of the world’s peaks over 8,000 metres in just over six months. He later led the first team to summit K2, the world’s second-highest mountain, in winter. 1:52 Nirmal Purja climbs world’s 14 highest peaks in record-breaking 189 days – video report “Records are made to be broken,” the former Gurkha and UKSF member told the Guardian in 2019 . “Someone one day will come along and be stronger. People are only limited by their imagination. If you don’t dream, then you won’t do it. Human beings are capable of doing amazing things.” The expedition included five Nepali climbers, as well as US, Pakistani, Omani and Chinese nationals. Another foreign climber was also part of the group, said Karrar Haidri, the vice-president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan. Elite Exped also confirmed the deaths of other expedition members, including his climbing partners and guides, Pur Bahadur Gurung (Yukta), a Nepali citizen, and Nima Sherpa. “Our deepest thoughts, prayers and heartfelt condolences are with their families, friends and loved ones,” the Elite Exped statement said. “No words can erase the pain of this unimaginable loss, and we ask that everyone respects their privacy as they grieve.” Map of Broad Peak On Friday, rescuers had said that four bodies had been found and efforts were under way to retrieve them despite the harsh weather. Among the victims were Nadhira Alharthy, the first Omani to climb Everest, and a US climber, Mallory Geis. View image in fullscreen Nadhira Alharthy, the first Omani to climb Everest, was also among the victims. Photograph: instagram/alharthynoor Trackers carried by the climbers showed a rapid loss of altitude, suggesting the team had been caught in an avalanche. Purja’s tracker, however, shifted location after the initial rapid descent. The GPS data suggested the avalanche occurred close to 9am local time at 6,579 metres (21,585ft), between camps two and three on the west ridge of the 8,047-metre mountain, the most popular ascent route. View image in fullscreen Broad Peak is the 12th highest mountain in the world at 8,051 metres. Photograph: Naveed Hussain/Alamy The British adventurer Bear Grylls said the news of Purja’s death was “heartbreaking for so many climbers around the world who had a relationship with this remarkable and unique man”. In the 2023 documentary Finding Michael, Purja and Grylls were enlisted to recover the body of Michael Matthews , the youngest Briton to climb Everest, who disappeared on the mountain in 1999. Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of them in the special forces. In 2018, he was awarded an MBE by the queen for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering. He also drew plaudits for twice risking his life to help others. The first time was while descending from Annapurna, when he led a rescue of fellow climber Chin Wui Kin, who had been separated from an accompanying expedition and left without food, water or oxygen for 40 hours. He later died in hospital. Less than a month later, Purja and his team rescued two climbers from a height of 8,400 metres, sacrificing their own supplementary oxygen to the climbers in need. “For me it’s not about ego,” he previously told the Guardian. “It’s about principles. You can’t call yourself a climber and not help in that situation.” Explore more on these topics Mountaineering Pakistan South and central Asia Avalanches Nepal news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

German Historian and Academic, Tarik Cyril Amar on Na-zi Imagery, and Ethnic Cleansing Apologia in Early 2000s Lviv. Eva Karene Bartlett , Jul 22, 2026, https://evakarenebartlett.substack.com/p/german-historian-and-academic-tarik?utm_source=post-email-title&publication_id=3046064&post_id=207930798&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=1ise1&triedRedirect=true&utm_medium=email Tarik Cyril Amar [ Tarik Cyril Amar ] lived for five years in Lviv, Ukraine, from 2001 on and off. He speaks fluent Russian and Ukrainian. A historian and author, Tarik has extensive knowledge, and first hand experience, on realities of Ukraine now whitewashed in Western corporate media, in particular the long festering and growing nationalism where Ukrainians nationalists—who committed war crimes, including ethnic cleansing in World War 2—are applauded and celebrated as “national heroes”. In our conversation, he also spoke of the lead role of his country Germany in expanding and fuelling the proxy war—in which the West has used Ukraine to fight Russia, with no actual regard for the lives of Ukrainians themselves. “It is the West that is using Ukraine as cannon fodder, and has been for years.” -Long history of Lviv support of Bandera and OUN “Even then, Lviv had a reputation as being a particularly patriotic, even nationalist, city. My personal experience at the time was that that was true, and that this tendency was on the rise. You had demonstrations celebrating the OUN (Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists in WW2). You found it in policies of public commemoration. Lviv has one of the largest monuments to Stepan Bandera in Ukraine, built or inaugurated during my time there. There was already a very consistent denial of the crimes of Ukrainian nationalists in WW2, the enormous massacres that they conducted systematically against the Poles. Nazi symbols in Lviv “You had the symbolism of the Waffen-SS division that the Nazis established in 1943. Lviv was the epicentre of that operation. Their symbolism, their coat of arms, that was there in the public space. You had the black and red of the OUN, that was prominent. You had attempts at building memorials in public spaces to the “heroism” of the nationalists. From what I can see now, it must have become much more aggressive. At the same time, there has been some resistance against forced mobilization in Lviv. On one side, there is this escalation of very strong nationalism that was already there. On the other, clearly the impact of the war is that some people are beginning to resist mobilization, even there.” -Polish demand for Ukraine to renounce the honouring of Ukrainian “nationalist heroes” doesn’t represent a change of Polish support to the war. The tension is old, the core of the tension is the systematic Ukrainian nationalist ethnic cleansing of Poles—estimates from 80,000-100,000 killed. “The killing is a message to make people leave, it’s a genocidal ethnic cleansing. What the Ukrainian nationalists did then, deliberately, systematically, and what the Israelis are doing now in Gaza, its a parallel: Commit genocide and massacres to drive people out. It is one of the things that Ukrainian nationalists will not acknowledge…it’s state policy in Ukraine to lie about this. The bigger story (regarding the recent Polish demand) is how successive Polish governments have always put the geopolitics of using Ukraine against Russia first. So there are these tensions. From time to time you get a blow up, like now with Zelensky. Has it made a difference in the way that they support Ukraine in this proxy war against Russia? It doesn’t.” -Germany in the lead in support for Ukraine and the proxy war on Russia “The war in Ukraine has always had this double aspect. On one side, superficially, it’s a war between Ukraine and Russia. But on the other side, and I think this is more important, it’s a proxy war, in which the West has used Ukraine to fight Russia. The lead Western power in this proxy war against Russia used to be the United States…Under Trump, while Washington could have made a serious contribution to end the war, that’s not what they’ve done. They’ve essentially Europeanized the war, they’ve washed their hands on the money that they have to spend on it, but are still supporting Ukraine in other ways—with intelligence, black ops, CIA connections, etc—and they’re still giving Ukraine weapons, but they make the Europeans pay for them. … The final outcome is a Western proxy war against Russia with Germany in the lead. What the German government, industry and arms manufacturers have done, they’ve intensified payments to Ukraine and military industrial cooperation cutting across the two countries: Things for the Ukrainian military industrial complex are being produced in Germany, or Germany companies are producing in Ukraine. That means that the Russians probably, very likely, are telling us the truth when they’re saying that significant Ukrainian attacks on Russia now can only be carried out because of German assistance . The Russians can point to very specific things that hurt them and that could not be done by Ukraine without (German assistance). From Russia’s perspective, there is an argument for striking at the hinterland, where these weapons and these supplies are coming from or which supports them, and that’s actually us (Germany).” Absurd Western media campaigns about defeating Russia “German war mongers have been saying for years, publicly, ‘We (Germany) have to enable Ukraine so that they can take the war home to Russia.. We need to give Ukraine the capacity to strike deep into Russia.’ Ukraine is doing that now, and we clearly are heavily involved in having created that capacity, and nurturing it and supporting it. There is clearly a coordinated media and information war campaign : Wall Street Journal, The Economist, Financial Times…they and the politicians are all doing the same things. “ They’re spreading this new story that Zelensky is producing, that Ukraine now shifts its war effort from the ground—where it is not successful–to mid range and long range drone and missile strikes against Russia. The idea is that—and this would be very unusual historically, as every expert knows—that by this particular air campaign alone, Ukraine will turn the tables and defeat Russia. You find this all over the Western public space now.” The narrative now being spread resembles earlier narratives about those miracle weapons —remember, when they got the HIMARS, the German tanks, and everybody was like, ‘Once we give them this system, they’re going to turn the war around!’ If Ukraine continues like this, that exerts pressure on the Russian leadership to counter-escalate. They’ve already started. What nobody in the West wants to acknowledge is that Russia still maintains escalation dominance, they can still escalate further beyond what Ukraine can bear or do .” – Russian willingness for negotiation, Western pushing proxy war “Right now there is a dead end. What the Europeans could have done, especially if they had coordinated with the Americans, is to nudge Ukraine, which is totally dependent on the West, and tel them, ‘We understand, you don’t want to officially lose the war, but if you want to come to a negotiated settlement, you must make certain concessions.’ That hasn’t happened. The attitude has been the opposite, which is let’s just feed more weapons and money into Ukraine, Ukraine will provide the people. It i s actually the West that is using Ukraine as cannon fodder, and has been for years.” Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook July 26, 2026 - Posted by Christina Macpherson | Uncategorized No comments yet. https://www.thefastmode.com/technology-s.text: Technologies Services Business Devices TFM Awards 2026 LiveX 27 Yettel Hungary Appoints Csaba Saranyik as New Director of Data & AI Sunday, 04 October 2026 23:01 Ray Sharma 1 2 3 4 5 (0 votes) 2.6 min read font size decrease font size increase font size Comment Csaba Saranyik will be returning to the company as Director of Data & AI at Yettel Hungary from October 1, 2026. With over 20 years of telecommunications and technology experience, he will be responsible for further developing the company's data and artificial intelligence strategy and supporting data-driven operations and innovation. Csaba Saranyik has worked in areas where business goals and technology solutions are closely intertwined. Previously, he spent nearly a decade at Telenor Hungary, the predecessor of Yettel, where he led customer value management and advanced analytics. Later, he led marketing activities targeting large enterprise customers at Slovak Telekom.
